utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, when we took the break yesterday, I said we would decide on the question of whether the witness could be asked about proportionality. Consistent with the decision that we took earlier in relation to another witness, the Chamber will rule that questions asked about proportionality may be put to the witness, and the reason is this: That ultimately whether a particular response was sufficiently disproportionate so as to negative self-defence is ultimately, and will always be, a matter for the Trial Chamber. But this witness can say whether, on the basis of the training that he had and his military experience, a particular response was proportionate or not proportionate. The legal characterisation of the response as being proportionate or disproportionate is a matter, and will always remain a matter, for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General, I want to ask just a couple of questions about the Bosnian Serb response to the attack on the Lukavica barracks, and then I have a couple more issues I want to talk to you about and then this direct examination will conclude. Yesterday, you gave us some hallmarks of what you, as a Canadian officer, would consider a proportionate response, and I want to take those up in turn. The Serbian response to the attack on the Lukavica barracks, was it a like-versus-like, I believe was the phrasing you used, response?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indirect fire from the Muslims was replied by indirect fire from the Serbians, but it was a lot more and not directed to the headquarters. It was just directed to the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And if I can just flesh out this idea of like being responded to by like for just a moment, does that mean to you that, for example, a rifle should be replied to by a rifle, a tank by a tank, and so forth; or if one finds a enemy tank in an open place, could one, without violating these principles, for example, call in an air-strike on that tank? Could you respond to that, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you found a tank in a field, it would not be unreasonable or unacceptable to use air or another asset to take care -- to deal with the tank, because you go through the process of, is it a military target. If you want to destroy the tank, use the best system you can to destroy the tank and also mitigate or minimise any collateral damage. So it's not unreasonable.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And then turning back to the response to the Lukavica barracks attack. Was proper attention paid by the Bosnian Serbs to minimising collateral damage in that response?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Are you able to generalise -- because I believe that you testified that there were a number of times when the Bosnian Serb forces would respond to fire within the city by the Bosnian Muslims. Can you, on any level of generality, say if the Serbian responses were typically proportionate or typically disproportionate; and, if you say yes to that, then I will ask you to elaborate a bit.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. And can you tell us, first of all, at what level of generality? Was this most of the responses, some of the responses, half of the responses, that you saw?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would generalise it by saying that most of the response was disproportionate. There was, if I could, please, an opinion by most of the people that I worked with that it was -- if one Muslim was killed-- or one Serbian was killed, we would probably expect about ten Muslims would be killed in response.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And when you say that most of the responses you saw were disproportionate, was there any particular way in which they were generally disproportionate? Was it in paying no attention to collateral consequences? Was it responding to non-military targets? Was it responding in unlike kind? Are you able to generalise about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, are you treating collateral damage as being parallel with a proportionate or disproportionate response? I don't necessarily see the two things as being the same. I mean, a response could be wholly proportionate and yet collateral damage is caused. It strikes me that the criteria for assessing the proportionality of a response doesn't necessarily have anything to do with collateral damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am using collateral damage as a hallmark of a proportionate response, and the reason that I'm doing so is I'm attempting to follow the methodology that was laid down by this Chamber in the direct examination of Major General Nicolai, where the Chamber directed me to first elicit from the witness the criteria that the witness would use to assess proportionality. Since General Fraser yesterday indicated that paying attention to or minimising collateral damage would be one of the things he would use in assessing proportionality, I am therefore asking him to apply his criteria to the topic. And, of course, I pay heed to what Your Honour said this morning, that, of course, this is for the Trial Chamber, and if the Trial Chamber's criteria do not match those of the witness, then of course the Trial Chamber will assess the matter differently. But, as I say, I'm trying to follow what I'll call the Nicolai methodology of having the witness give the criteria, then asking the witness to apply those criteria to the facts he observed while in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. But it wouldn't be correct to say that the Trial Chamber had laid down the methodology. That was Mr. Nicolai's approach, as it appears to be the approach of the brigadier as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I take that correction, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General, the question that was pending was whether there was any way in which Bosnian Serb responses to Muslim attacks were disproportionate or whether they varied in that disproportionality and the manner of their disproportionality.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My observation was that the Serb response was disproportionate. It was greater.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Changing topics now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: At that level of generality, it is not helpful. I think he has to say in what way. Ultimately, we'll assess it. It's for the Trial Chamber to assess it ultimately. But he has had experience; he has had training in this field, If his evidence is to be of assistance to us, it has to be given at a more empirical level, it seems to me, at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: In your last response, General, you said: "My observation was that the Serb response was disproportionate," and then you added the sentence: "It was greater." When you say "It was greater," can you elaborate on that a bit more; and, if possible, incorporate into your answers specific observations you made while serving with the United Nations in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My experience was that in regards to sniping, if a Serbian civilian was killed, we would receive -- expect a lot more Muslims killed as a response to that, and, again, the general opinion was ten to one. As a result of the attack on Lukavica barracks, which was a series of mortar rounds coming out from the Muslim side, the artillery that came back from the Serbians was extensive and it lasted for quite some time. It was disproportionate to what the Lukavica barracks received actually in the way of shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Is that helpful, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So we had the Muslims using mortar rounds in their attack on the barracks and the response was with artillery. It "was extensive and it lasted for quite some time." Is it the fact that artillery was used or the extent of it and the duration that would make it disproportionate, in your view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, the attack on Lukavica barracks was against the corps headquarters and the response was directed to the city, and the response was not directed, in my opinion, to a military target. You know, the way I would have looked at it would have been, if you can find the Muslim mortar base-plate position that shot the rounds at the Lukavica barracks, that would be legitimate and proportional. The response, though, was just a general firing of artillery back at the city and for some time. So it wasn't just one salvo; it was multiple salvos over and over again. It was -- again, what was the target on the ground? I couldn't determine what the target was on the ground. It seemed to be more general, just aimed at the city. And there was an awful lot more coming in than the rounds that were coming out of the city that went after Lukavica barracks. In my opinion, from my training, I would question what the target was and was it proportional, because it was just a continuous barrage coming at the city for some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: General, can I ask you to clarify this, because it seems to me that your first response to counsel's question was that it was the weaponry and the duration that constituted the disproportionality of the response. You said, if I'm not mistaken, that the fact that artillery was used in response to mortar attacks was part of it, and the other part of it was that it lasted for some days. And then, in response to Judge Robinson's questions, you then added that it was rather the indiscriminate nature of the response that constituted the disproportionality. Now, which is it? Is it one or the other or is it both, really? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was just waiting for the screen. It is, in fact, both, and as a military officer, our training is not -- it's a whole bunch of factors that have you to combine all together. Proportionality is only one factor that must be considered in conjunction with the other factors; military necessity, military -- was it a military target, collateral damage. I mean, it's an equation that's all added together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. But we need exactly all the elements in that equation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just rephrase it again to make sure that I'm clear on what I said. The Muslims fired at a military target called Lukavica barracks headquarters. No issues there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did they hit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the vicinity of -- I mean, again, in my opinion, it was a legitimate target, military target. There were civilians around it, but the rounds landed in the area of the headquarters, because we were getting reports from French soldiers who were actually at the headquarters that they were under mortar attack, which was coming out of the city. So they just happened to be in the spot where it was a Serbian military target, and that was okay in that sense. Because we didn't assess that the Muslims were firing at the French soldiers; they were firing at the Serbian headquarters. Military firing at military, so that was okay. The response, though, the response that came back, was not fired at what we could assess as military targets. So that's one criteria that didn't seem to be met. It didn't appear to have looked at collateral damage; that's another criteria for returning fire. And it was not like, you know, you fire four rounds, you fire four rounds back; it was there was a tremendous volume of fire that came back and it was sustained for some time. So, yet again, it appeared, again from our point of view, as disproportionate, too. So the three criteria didn't seem to be met with the response from the Muslim side: military target, proportionality, and consideration for collateral damage for civilians who were in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. For further clarification, I would need to ask you: Were the military -- the Bosnian military targets, were they accessible? Could that have been detected, where they were? Was it possible to hit them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In short, no. The Muslim mortars would move around the city and they would fire -- making it very, very difficult for the Serbs to reply because they were intermingled and mixed in with civilians. And they did that purposely because it would make it hard, and if there was a response, it would be, you know, putting civilians at risk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The fact that the Bosnian sides were roaming around in the city and firing their mortar shots, would that have any impact on your assessment of the proportionality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In short, yes, it would. From my experience, because you can't find the fire unit that fired the shot and because it was moving around and inside a civilian area, as a soldier, I would not be able to fire back at all. I would have to just accept it, because, A, I couldn't find the target; B, the potential for collateral damage to civilians, it would preclude me from firing back at that target. It ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You just, in response to Judge Harhoff, spoke of the three criteria of military target, proportionality, and consideration of collateral damage for civilians who were in the area. But I find that a little confusing, because we are talking about criteria for determining proportionality, but you have included proportionality among the criteria. Your three criteria, I repeat, were military target, proportionality, and consideration for collateral damage. It's not clear to me how -- it's not helpful to have proportionality as one of the three criteria for determining proportionality, unless you were speaking of three criteria for something else, something other than proportionality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me give you another example. If there was a sniper up in a tower, the ideal thing would be to use another sniper to take out that individual. Some people would probably use a tank. They could use an airplane and destroy the entire tower. You have taken out the tower -- you have taken out the sniper and the sniper was a military target. You could have satisfied the collateral damage. If there are no civilians around, you just destroy the tower. But was that proportional? In my training, that would be disproportional. You don't need to destroy the entire tower to take out one sniper. There are other systems you can use to do that in a far more judicious way. It is not black and white. It is a judgement call. And I spent all my time making judgement calls to apply those three criteria and try to apply the minimum amount of force to achieve the effect that we need to achieve based on military targets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would your military manual contain something on this issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On proportionality, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I tried to explain, it's -- you try to do like with like and you don't try to use excessive --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no. I'm talking about a manual. Most armies have a manual, and I was trying to find out whether the manual for the Canadian Army would have something on proportionality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It does. All right. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Just to be clear, before we leave this topic, General, when you talk about collateral damage, what sorts of people are we talking about as far as collateral damage goes? Who are the victims of collateral damage?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, collateral damage is more than people. It's places and things. For example, schools, churches, other areas that may be designated as places and things that we're in the allowed to shoot at. And there are rules about what we can and cannot shoot. So collateral damage, again, is a generic term that has also further definitions and requirements. It is most frequently used to talk about civilians, people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm going to leave this topic now and I'm going to ask you about the command and control of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, the Bosnian Serb forces, during your time in Sarajevo. Do you have an opinion as to who -- let me back up. Yesterday, you gave some testimony and you mentioned an officer with the last name of Indic; you testified, I believe, about higher Serbian leadership in Pale. That's the origin of the question I'm about to ask you, which is: Who, in your opinion, during your time in Sarajevo, was effectively in command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and what are the reasons for that opinion, if you have one?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my assessment that the corps commander was in command and in control of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And what was the name of that corps commander in the latter part of your tour?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: We talked a little bit yesterday about protests.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm going to the court officer at this time to call up ter number 2065. And, Your Honours, for purposes of the record, this will be evidence that is relating to scheduled sniping incident number 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You asked the witness, who, in your opinion, during your time in Sarajevo, was effectively in command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and what are the reasons for that opinion. He has stated that, in his view, General Milosevic was in command, but he hasn't given the reason for saying why, in his view, he was effectively in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: That's why I called for the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The documents. I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm going to have questions based on the documents that will flesh this out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: On the screen in front of you, General, there should be a letter. Do you recognise this document, first of all?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, what this document is.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a protest from General Rose to Dr. Karadzic regarding sniping incidents on the 8th of October, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And, again, for purposes of the record, Your Honour, scheduled sniping incident number 1, the evidence has been that it occurred on the 8th of October, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Is this a kind of letter that was -- when you testified about protest letters, is this one of the types of things you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. Following the mailing -- this letter has a date on it. Could you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's dated the 9th of October, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And do you know, was there a meeting which followed this letter with Serbian leadership?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Let me show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If I could ask the registrar to display ter number 2067, and in particular e-court page 2 of that document, paragraph number 5. But if we could see the first page first because I want the witness to see the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General, on the screen in front of you now there is a document. Can you tell us, first of all, what kind of document is this?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a summary of a meeting between General Mladic and General Rose near Pale. It's typical for summarising meetings that were conducted between the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The first sentence under "Summary" says: "Rose met with Mladic today near Pale." For those of us, like me, who are not good at reading military times and dates, is there information here that will tell us what "today" is?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we just blow that up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can we expand the boxed portion just a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Does that help, General?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. It would have been on the 10th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And if we could please see e-court page 2, numbered paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And I'll just pause for a moment and let you and everyone else read numbered paragraph 5. All right. Now, I want to continue with this topic. You indicate, or the document indicates, that it is General Rose taking up this shooting on a tram with fairly senior leaders. What sorts of incidents would be taken up with these relatively senior leaders?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sniping was a major issue that my general and General Rose would raise with the warring factions because of the psychological impact it had on the population. And also, after a while, incidents would slowly build up and it would have to generate into a major discussion like this one - and I was at this meeting - where, in fact, we would try to get the situation under more control. But sniping was a major discussion point between the factions that we were dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And I'm going to show you another document relative to sniping. Before I do that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsel, sorry, could you please ask the witness to elaborate a little on this; namely, the question of whether sniping was always a topic on the agenda for all the meetings between the UNPROFOR and the warring parties, also the Bosnian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General, was sniping more frequently -- which warring faction was spoken to more frequently or was the recipient of more protests regarding sniping?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked about sniping, we talked about shelling, and we talked about freedom of movement with all the factions. We talked about a number of different issues that were affecting either side. We talked about more issues with the Serb side than we did with the Muslim side because the Muslims, in this case, were inside of Sarajevo and they were the ones being contained. Freedom of movement was affected by them. But we did go and talk to them about issues about shelling, issues about sniping against, you know, non-military targets, for example. The discussions were wide-ranging and we talked to both parties, but in this particular case we were talking to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Just to try and follow up a little more on Judge Harhoff's question. Are you able to say that one side or the other did more sniping on civilians that had to be addressed by the United Nations in meetings and letters and so forth?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We dealt more with the Serbs on sniping than we did on the Muslims on sniping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I guess my concern was just to establish through this witness that sniping was not just something that was, you know, discussed every now and then, but it was always a very important part of the agenda for all meetings. That was my concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And that may vary by the type of meeting, but I can explore that with a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could you?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What we're looking at now, General Fraser, is minutes of a meeting by General Rose. Give us an idea of how senior within the UN hierarchy General Sir Michael Rose was at this time.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Rose commanded all the UN troops in Bosnia, the actual country. He worked for General Dilaprow [phoen], who was the force commander for all of UNPROFOR. The fact is that General Rose would deal with those issues that were most significant to the country, and he would limit his engagements principally with the senior leadership on the Serbian side, either General Mladic, Dr. Karadzic, or on the Muslim, with the president, the vice-president, the prime minister. And corps commanders were the purview of my general to talk to, the two warring faction corps commanders. But when it came to certain issues that could be significantly destabilising or an escalatory matter for the city, as it pertained to Sector Sarajevo or the DMZ, General Rose would certainly get engaged to try and keep the situation -- implore the leadership to get control of the situations. In this particular case, it was sniping. We would be talking about shelling, we would be talking about other -- freedom of movement, utilities, just, you know, things that people need to go about their lives, because we were there to protect the people as much as anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And so a meeting like the one we've got the minutes of in front of us, this is not a daily occurrence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is becoming really impossible to follow. I'm trying to follow the interpretation, and in French it's very difficult, it's extremely fast, and there is a big gap. We're a few lines away from what is being said and it's very difficult. Can we please slow the pace. Please slow the pace so that interpretation is possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Isailovic. I think both the witness and Mr. Docherty will have heard that. It's really a complaint. The dialogue, it's too fast. Please observe a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: A meeting like the one we've got the minutes in front of us, this was -- how frequently were high-level meetings like this convened?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not very often. This was only when the situation was getting grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What about corps level, one level down? How frequently were there meetings to talk about sniping, talk about shelling, talk about freedom of movement, at the level of the general, whose military assistant you were?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were more frequent than what General Rose would engage. And then the battalion commanders under us would have even more discussions with their counterparts, the brigade commanders. So the lower down you got, the more the dialogue was almost continuous. And my general would engage with the corps commanders again on issues that required their attention to keep the situation in check and under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I will tender the two documents that I have been using, ter number 2065, the letter from General Rose to Dr. Karadzic, and ter number 2067, which is on the monitor just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: They're admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Ter number 02065 will be admitted as Exhibit P204, and 02067 will be admitted as P205, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And if we could now see 65 ter number 01973, which I believe is already in evidence as Prosecution Exhibit 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, before you move on to the next subject. General, you said regarding the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, yes, that General Milosevic was de facto commander, that he had control. But then you are also talking about meetings of Lieutenant General Michael Rose with Dr. Karadzic or General Mladic. During those meetings or after these meetings, General Mladic denied what was happening with snipers or shelling. It seems to me, therefore, that the one having effective control on the operations was him. So how can you explain that particular situation? On the one hand we have General Mladic himself who seems to be in control and on the other hand we have General Milosevic who also has control? Is there a contradiction or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't see a contradiction. I see a higher commander -- a higher commander, General Mladic's intent and direction being adhered to and followed by General Milosevic. In the military chain of command, the guy at the top gives out his orders, his intent, and the subordinates follow that; and they, in turn, give out orders and intent and they follow that. So it is a series and a degrees of command and competency. At the corps level, when we would go to the corps commander and protest either sniping, shelling, freedom of movement, normally afterwards we would get an improvement in the situation. But over time, there may be too many situations that would be unacceptable to General Rose and the -- amelioration or the situation on the ground would be too tense and he would get engaged and go up to Milosevic's bosses on this side - it would be General Mladic - to say, "You have to take this and be more serious about it and slow it down." And it was not uncommon for both parties to say they didn't do it. That was always -- the opening statement was: "We didn't do it." And then you would just argue and then they would go away and things would get a little better in most cases. Yes, Mladic was the boss. Yes, he had significant control and command because he was directing operations not only in Sarajevo but for the rest of the country. But within that little box called Sarajevo, General Milosevic was the guy in command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. I'm sorry, I was waiting for the end of the interpretation so that I could understand well. You say that General Milosevic was de facto commander. According to your military experience, can you have a commander who is also a pawn, so to speak? He has the title but maybe not the control. So can we have a commander who in fact is not really, de facto, the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure it's as simple as that, because all subordinate commanders must follow the orders of their superiors. In short, if a subordinate has a problem with the superior commander's orders, he always has the option of quitting, if he cannot do it. But the chain of command is designed that the subordinates execute the orders of their commanders within the intent of the commander -- the superior commander's direction. It's a hierarchy and that's how we operate. I wouldn't phrase it as a pawn. It is a chain of command where we would have a dialogue with our boss about how to do things based on the information on the ground, and that's how the military is structured. I'm not sure I have answered your question, but that's how I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Yes, you have answered my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I called for the wrong ter number. The ter number I need is actually 1973, and I would ask if that could be shown, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General Fraser, do you recognise the document that's on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What is this document, please?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is an agreement on the elimination of sniping activities in the Sarajevo region.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And it might be off -- who has signed this document?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is signed by General Karavelic, the commander of the Muslim corps; General Mladic, the commander of the Serbian corps; and General Rose.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If I could ask the registrar to scroll down because there's a date beside General Rose's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: There's a date to the right of General Rose's signature. Can you tell us what that is, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the 14th of August, 1994. And it's also signed by Viktor Andreev, who was the political advisor for General Rose.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Are you aware of how this document, this agreement, came into being? What was the genesis of it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there at the time when the negotiations took place, but it was as a result of the escalating sniping incidents around Sarajevo, and the intervention of General Rose to try to get control of the situation and bring things back down to a more reasonable level.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, following up on this question of command and control, is the signature on this document by General Karavelic and General Mladic, the two corps commanders, something from which you can draw any conclusions about who had control over sniping in the Sarajevo area?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally, after these types of meetings and agreements, in this particular case the situation would get better, which would indicate to me that both of these gentlemen had control over their troops and were able to pass down orders to stop the sniping.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did the United Nations do any studies into the effectiveness of this Anti-Sniping Agreement?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The French did keep statistics on sniping, how many people were shot on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm going to ask to look at that study now, and I will ask the registrar to call up ter number 2011, e-court page 4. Before I get into that, at this time, Your Honour, I will tender ter number 1973, the Anti-Sniping Agreement of 14 August 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P206, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: On the screen in front of you now, General Fraser, is a document with a number of dates on the left-hand margin and then some numbers in the body. Do you recognise this document, is my first question?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a summation of wounded/killed of Serbs and Muslims for the Sarajevo area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And this is a little -- might be a little hard to interpret. Can you just walk us through what this document shows or how this data is organised and how we should read it.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we would normally do is track, in this particular case, the number of sniping incidents in the city, where they took place; who was wounded, in the first column, which was Muslims; how many Muslims were killed; how many Serbs were wounded; how many Serbs were killed. We would take that information. We would use it to conduct our discussions with the applicable warring factions to say -- go to them with empirical data and facts of incidents so that it would be a focused discussion. We would give them that information, and the objective was to reduce and to eliminate sniping against civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, on the far left series of numbers, it's labelled "BiH Wounded." Is that Bosnia and Herzegovina wounded?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Two questions about that. First of all, we see -- rather than months, we see specific dates on the left-hand side. In other words, this doesn't appear to be a linear sort of chart. The specific dates, does that mean that individuals were killed or wounded on those specific dates?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Up near the top we are seeing single-digit numbers. Later on, for example, July 29, August 5, and August 19, we are seeing double-digit numbers. What conclusion, if any, can you draw about the effectiveness of the Anti-Sniping Agreement from the data that is in the chart in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, before it took place there was a significant problem, and after it, there still continues to be a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Are the numbers after it smaller or larger or the same as the numbers that gave rise to the agreement in the first place?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right afterwards the number spikes to, I think -- it look like 12 there, and then it drops back to the levels that existed predating the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And from this data can you draw any conclusions about whether the corps commanders who signed the Anti-Sniping Agreement had control over sniping in the Sarajevo theatre?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if they had control or if they ignored the document that they -- the agreement they signed. But there was no effect of the negotiations or the agreement based on these facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a couple of other documents relative to sniping.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Before I do that, Your Honour, I'll tender ter number 2011, the study on the effectiveness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P207, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And now, Mr. Registrar, if I could please ask for ter number 01939.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General, I'll ask you to take a moment and look at that document. When you've familiarised yourself with it and are ready to proceed, please indicate that.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What kind of a document is this?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a direction to all the units inside the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps from the deputy commander indicating that there is a problem; that the reports that are being written are not being reviewed by the commanders, the subordinate commanders, and the direction is that the commanders will personally get involved, or the Chief of Staff, to make sure that the orders from higher are being applied, and that the reports that are coming back are accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, a few minutes ago you were talking about the chain of command in the armed forces. Does this document bear on the discussion and on the role or the limits on the -- excuse me. Does this document bear on a discussion of chain of command and of subordinates' relationships with higher officers in a military organisation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay. Could you elaborate on that, please, and tell us how this sheds light on that discussion.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document indicates to me that the deputy commander of the corps was unhappy, not satisfied, that the subordinates were either following his orders or the subordinate commanders were actively engaged in controlling their troops in what was going on. This document really is a measure, an order to get the chain of command more engaged in establishing control over what was going on at that time, which was July of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And then before -- first of all, Your Honour, I will tender this document, ter number 01939.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P208, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And then I have one last topic that I want to cover with you, General. But before I do, I want to circle back to something we were talking about a little while ago, which was the response to the attack on the Lukavica barracks. Your discussion of criteria for returning fire, your discussion of proportionality, was heavily oriented towards using the response to the Lukavica barracks attack as an example. Were there other like situations that you observed during your time in Sarajevo where Muslim fire from within the city received a response from the Bosnian Serb side that you would consider not to meet the criteria you've explained for the responsible use of military force?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any other specific incidents that I could relate to you right now other than just my general impression of all the incidents. So I can't be more specific than I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What about your general impression? What would your general impression be?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My general impression was the Serbs were definitely in control of all the movement and the situation inside the city. They used all their means available to keep control and control freedom of movement, control the psychological aspects of the city, through the sniping and through shelling, be it mortars mainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The last topic I want to talk with you about, and then this direct examination will be over, are you familiar with the term from your time in Sarajevo "modified air bomb"?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. That was something that came up at the very end of my tenure in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What is a modified air bomb?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a bomb that has some sort of makeshift apparatus put onto it so that it can be used as a vehicle that can fly but has no guidance system. You just aim it, you launch it off, and it will go wherever the ballistic capabilities and the aerodynamic capabilities of this improvised device are. And it lands based on if it runs out the fuel, or, more likely, the aerodynamics of it are it just flops down. It has no military value, in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Have you ever seen such a contraption before you went to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Ever seen one since?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You're a military office -- a senior military officer with decades of experience in the Canadian Army. You have had training on what kind of weapons are appropriate for what kind of battlefield situations. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Was there ever a time when you, as a commander, would say, "Send me the modified air bombs. I need one."

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did you ever see modified air bombs on the Bosnian Muslim side of the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did you ever see launchers for modified air bombs on the Bosnian Muslim side of the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Do you have an opinion from your time in Sarajevo as to the effect these devices had on the psychology of the civilian population of the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were psychologically very devastating for the people to hear that these things existed, and if they did fire, my only experience was it sent shudders through all of us, including the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: How does the explosive capacity of one of these devices compare with a mortar round? We've been talking a lot about mortar rounds and that's why I ask.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were normally larger, much larger.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsel, can I just ask you to complete this examination regarding the weaponry, because we were told a couple of days ago about a gun called M-85, a machine-gun, I understand. Could you ask the witness about the range and precisionness of this weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General, are you familiar with the weapon that Judge Harhoff is asking about? I think it might be an M-84 but perhaps M-85, automatic-fire rifle?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with the M-85.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay. What about the M-84?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those numbers don't mean anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Isailovic to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. I am Branislava Isailovic, attorney-at-law and member of the Paris Bar Association. I'm the legal counsel for General Milosevic in these preceding. You know he is the accused in these proceedings. You know the procedure because you've also testified in the Galic case. We will now proceed with the cross-examination and we will talk together of the various issues that you already discussed with the Prosecution. I would like to discuss with you a few matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To begin with, I would like to ask my case manager to pull up on the screen a 65 ter map, 2927. This is a document -- a document that was admitted as a Prosecution Exhibit P194.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for this map - it will take a while - I would like to begin with a few questions on your military career, or, rather, the experience you gained in Sarajevo. In the statement you gave in 1997, but also yesterday during your testimony, you talked about the generals for whom you worked, do you remember, Generals Soubirou and Gobillard?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember Generals Soubirou and Gobillard, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: They were generals from the French army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. General Soubirou was the deputy commander of the 6th Armoured Division and General Gobillard was the commander of the 11th Parachute Division. That was the 11th Parachute, not 12th.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You were in Sector Sarajevo, and as far as the command for Bosnia and Herzegovina, I believe the British generals were commanding; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Sector Sarajevo was part of Bosnia and Herzegovina which was broken down into a number of sectors, and General Rose was the commander there when I got there and he was subsequently replaced by General Rupert Smith.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So there were, let's say, cultural differences, from a military point of view, between those two sets of generals; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were culturally different as British and French, but they shared a common bond as being soldiers in arms.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: As an assistant to Generals Soubirou and Gobillard your role was, among other things, to translate, so to speak, to be a link between those two cultures. Because you're a Canadian yourself and I believe that you speak fluently both languages, English and French. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say it's a bit of a stretch to say that was a conduit, a link, between two cultures. They were able to communicate quite effectively themselves. They did not need me to translate for them. General Soubirou spoke very good English; General Rose spoke very good French. General Gobillard and General Rupert Smith didn't speak as well, but they were able to communicate effectively. And I just happened to be there because it was a UN force and I was just the military assistant. And yes, at the time I could speak very good French. I would say in the ten years since then, my French skills have actually diminished.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But regarding those cultural differences, from a military standpoint, could you elaborate on what they were exactly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Has he said there were cultural differences? Ms. Isailovic, I'm not sure whether he agreed with your proposition.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. He mentioned military cultures, not cultural differences but differences from the point of view of military culture. Maybe we could see the statement. He believe he said something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, the statement you gave in 1997, maybe I could refer you to that part of your statement, because for me it is a very interesting part. General, would you like to see that part of your statement in which you mentioned those differences in the military culture of the French Generals and the British Generals?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If that's in the statement and you wish to show him, show it to him. It's not a matter for him.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll keep that question for later because we have the map. It takes a long time to pull it up on the screen, so let's have a look at it. Mr. Registrar, could we enlarge the map. We need to see also the whole top part of the map. Could we enlarge it, or zoom. Yes, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: General, we discussed this map yesterday; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that there are various markings already drawn on this map. For instance, within the blue line, starting from the top left part, we have "111 vbbr." This is the biggest mark. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that these are the zones of responsibility of the units belonging to the 1st Corps of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the map shows and that would be consistent with what was happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that there are various markings on the map? We have some letters that are bigger than others and, of course, smaller ones. But at any rate, can we agree that they covered the whole territory within the blue line?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This map would indicate there are a series of units that cover the area inside and around the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree on the fact that it is the 12th Division of the 1st Corps of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina which was within that blue line?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I see where you see the 12th Division on that map. I don't see that. Can you help me out here? I see brigades; I don't see a division.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: General, in fact, I wanted you to tell me if you recalled that at the time there was a division called the 12th Division whose commander was, I believe, a general, General Fikret Prevljak?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the 1st Muslim Corps under Karavelic, the brigades, and I do remember General Fikret. I do not recall that he was a division commander. My recollection was he was a brigade commander, commanding, if it's the same guy, commanding the Mount Igman area, just on the southern side of the airport.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, you said that you saw the various locations of the brigades, is that correct, within this blue line on the map?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can read where the brigades were based on the map. I did not personally, nor did my general, deal with brigades. We dealt exclusively with the corps commander and the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: General, I would like to go back to your long experience as a military officer. Please tell us if these locations of the various brigades also included the locations of military objectives, targets. I'm talking about, for instance, the headquarters of all these units, again located in this blue line.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: To your opinion, although I'm pretty sure I already know the answer because you mentioned the Lukavica barracks a moment ago which was the headquarters of the army of Republika Srpska, were all these installations military targets?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Lukavica barracks was -- I knew where that was and it was a military target. I could tell you that the Muslim corps headquarters was downtown. It was a target but it was completely surrounded by other civilian buildings. It would be very difficult, I would say, to engage, and it never was in the entire time I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Let's remain theoretical. You took the example of the Lukavica barracks, saying that it was the headquarters and that it could be a military target, a legitimate military target. Could the same criteria be applied to any headquarters?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And the fact that a headquarters is located within an area where there are civilian installations, does that cancel the military nature of that headquarters?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does not cancel the military nature of the headquarters. It makes the prosecution of any action against that headquarters extremely difficult, if not almost impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Let's now move on and talk about specific example, the Lukavica barracks. Did you know that Lukavica was a residential area in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: If I continue along the lines of your reasoning, can it be said that it would be hard to assess the military nature of this headquarters, which, in fact, is located in a residential neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Lukavica barracks is a legitimate military target, as I would define it. The fact that it was also in a neighbourhood is a significant consideration when you're talking about collateral damage. But compared to its Muslim counterpart, it was much -- it was a cleaner situation, but it was no less difficult because of the potential for collateral damage with the residents and the civilians around the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: General, may I conclude from this that it would have been very difficult to fight in urban settings, in general?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fighting in urban settings is a very, very hard thing for a military to do, any military. Fighting around Sarajevo during the time I was there, it was particularly difficult for both parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, it's time for the break, and we will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, General, we just finished before the break when you were saying that combat in Sarajevo during your mandate was extremely difficult for both warring factions, and we'll continue on this. Could you please look at the map on the screen and focus on the location of the 105th Brigade, the 152nd Brigade, and the 115th Brigade. Can we agree to say that the areas of responsibility of those three brigades were located in a very dense part of town? We see a lot of buildings, I mean, in this brownish colour. So can we agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The areas where the brigades are includes a very dense part of Sarajevo, but it would depend on where they actually deployed their troops within that area. And I can't agree just based on this. It is a particularly difficult area, but there are some open areas in that region.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: General, does the location of these brigades and their headquarters also involve other military facilities which normally accompany any unit being deployed?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And did you acquire any information on this during your stay in Sarajevo as General Gobillard's and General Soubirou's military assistant?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you be more specific? Because I did not normally deal with brigades; I dealt specifically -- or mainly with the corps headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was rather calling on your general knowledge, and you answered affirmatively. Then I asked you a practical question on Sarajevo at that time, when you were the military assistant to these two generals. If you don't know, I mean, of course you can answer by just saying that you don't know.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Earlier when we talked about proportionality -- and we accepted to discuss this with you, and it's an important issue, but you have a lot of experience in this area and you have very specific knowledge concerning this. And you said that a response when you're being attacked from a densely populated place is very difficult. So my question is: What can a commander do when he is placed in such a situation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander in a situation like that, hypothetically, has to consider what I described earlier - military necessity, proportionality, collateral damage. In some cases, the commander would not be able to reply, as we did not reply every time that we, in the UN, were being shot at. Because although we could identify a military target, because of proportionality and collateral damage, we could not satisfy those conditions; therefore, we did not fire back because of the surrounding areas. It's that difficult. But having said that, we will go back and protest to the party that did that, as our reply, our response.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: General, defending the territory that you occupy, is that a military necessity?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the territory that you're defending. In the case of Sarajevo where the Muslims were defending the city, yes, that was required. You asked me: "Defending the territory that you occupy, is that a military necessity?" I mean, the short answer would be yes. But, you know, why are you defending the territory in the first place? I think I'm inferring from your question: Why defend Sarajevo? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree by saying that it's a military necessity for the two military factions, the two parties involved?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In short, yes. But the circumstances where we found ourselves, looking at this map, the difference was what got us to that point would have been the Serbs doing enough advance and offence, and they got to the point where they couldn't take the city so they stopped and dug in. So you had two forces opposing each other, with the city being the objective; one to defend it and one to get it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So if we look at the map again, can we agree to say that that blue line represents the position of the BiH army and the red line is the position of Republika Srpska? Do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And behind that red line, to your knowledge and using your memory, were there any territories that were inhabited by civilians?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Behind that red line, were there civilian objectives or facilities also, targets?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I understand "civilian objectives or facilities, targets." Civilians are not targets. Can you rephrase your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm thinking about civilians that could be -- I'm using the Geneva Protocol, you know, civilian objectives. It's a word that describes not just people but also buildings, facilities, of a civilian nature.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the objective is to take a building or a city, for example, the condition that the commander has to make sure is that he doesn't engage "non-combatants," is the term we would use, or civilians who were not part of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: General, does this apply to all factions?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So what about the location of the BiH army and its brigades, the ones I mentioned earlier when we started?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their problem was accentuated by the fact that you had a Serbian corps surrounding the city, indicated by that red line, and they were defending the city from the Serbian advance. And to do that, they found themselves actually interspersed amongst the civilians. Again, this is the characteristic of urban warfare. It is very hard for both the defender and the attacker.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, General. I'm not a military expert. I know nothing about the military. But let's talk about military advantage. In the end, isn't it a huge military advantage to have all your facilities interspersed within civilian objectives?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In one sense it is an advantage because it makes it harder to engage, and in the other sense you are actually exposing civilians to greater risk, which commanders have to take into consideration too. So it's a -- you've got two considerations. There's an advantage and the disadvantage.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So, General, we can talk about a reasonable commander and the standards used by a reasonable commander, and so here's my question: What does this reasonable commander do? Does he just give up or continue and pursue defending the interests of his party, pursuing its own military necessity?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A reasonable commander would probably consider the risk to civilians and try to mitigate that risk to civilians and not put them into harm's way when he is, in fact, in a conflict with another military force. And in the event that a military commander faces another military commander who has interspersed himself in amongst civilians, it makes his job far more difficult, and, as I said earlier, in some cases it would prevent him from engaging that other military commander because of the potential for harming civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I think I understand things better now and I fully agree with you regarding what you said on July 5th, 2002, when you were cross-examined in the Galic case. On page 11238 - I will read this - these are your words: "[In English] How do you get inside to a target that is surrounded by non-combatants? It is a soldier's worst nightmare."

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely agree. I said it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let's go back to the map. Earlier you said that the red line -- well, looking at the red line, we see that Sarajevo was encircled. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But there's an entire part located close to where we have the marking "102nd Brigade," where the airport is located, close to the airport. Do you see that part of the map?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And there, the red line is cut. It stops.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could please have on the map, if you could use the pen, and point to the airport so that we can --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, I'm asking for the usher to come and help move the map up so we can see the airport and the surroundings. Please scroll up slightly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, General, you annotated a few locations with that pen. I'm sure you're familiar with the use of this electronic pen and how we mark maps now. So could you please first mark on the map where the airport is located.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Isailovic. Earlier you said to the witness that the red line is cut, it stops, and he affirmed that. May I be shown where that is on the map? And that's where the red line is cut?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The red line goes -- can you just clear off the map again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Where is the cut in the red line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there is a gap, in fact, right here. Do you see where the 155 number is, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. Yes, yes. I see 155.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is an actual gap between there, between the red lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But there are several gaps in the red lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So what was the significance of the cut in the red line? I'm asking you, Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It just denoted where in fact -- the airport actually separated the two warring factions, and there was a little gap in there where, in fact, the city wasn't completely encircled. There was a little area that was left open. And it was during that -- it's in that area, and using the airport, that in fact ground supply convoys for the city came in and out. And in fact that's how the Muslims actually got in and out of the city, too, through the infamous tunnel that went underneath the airport and through that gap that went from the 155 marking, somewhere in and around there, and went across into Butmir. That's how you got in and out of the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Proceed, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So you talked about the tunnel. You mentioned that. So I no longer need to ask the question of whether there was a tunnel or not. So could you please continue with the exercise we were engaged in and actually circle the airport.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And please place an A, letter A, for "airport."

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, to your knowledge and according to what you remember, where was the entry and the exit of that tunnel located, that tunnel that was actually going all the way under -- that was going to the runway of the airport?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never actually saw the -- got into the tunnel. The area that I was told where it was, the entrance or the exit, there was one somewhere around there, and the other one was somewhere around here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Both sides say there is an exit and an entry. Now, is it true to say that after the exit, so I'm talking about the exit on the west side, that after that, this is territory controlled by the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: General, military-wise, this is quite an important means of communication between units that are inside the blue line that we mentioned earlier and the territory covered by the 104th Brigade that can take us to Mount Igman. So this is a very -- a quite important military link; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And as far as you remember - so if you don't remember anything, you know, just tell us - the territory after Mount Igman, did that provide sufficient depth to the unit of the 1st Corps, to the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I'm not sure I understand what you mean by "depth."

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it's a military expression, military jargon. I'm not teaching you military terms, but I learned this. I investigated military jargon. If you say what went behind, at your back, you've got enough depth, you've got a good amount of territory, it's an advantage military-wise to be able to have a safe back, if I can say so.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that particular case I would agree with the use of the term "depth." But in this particular case, that was the route in and out of Sarajevo. So it's not depth; it's just the route.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But there we had the Igman road, and this road was controlled by the BiH army unit; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. And it was extensively used by the Muslim civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Civilians. Was it also used by the military of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So then can it be considered as a legitimate military target?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can, as long as you don't kill civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So we'll come back to the problem of how to make a difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you were asked to show where Lukavica is. Could you please do that again on this map and place an L where Lukavica is.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you blow up that map for me, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I think we have to first keep this one. So let's erase the L, please. Erase the L. The A is also erased, unfortunately, so please place the A again, as in "airport."

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we please have this map tendered, and I would like a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D44, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, we have to erase everything in order to be able to zoom the map, and we just need a slight zoom.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see where Lukavica is located now that it's been zoomed in?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Please place an L next to Lukavica, and then an I on Ilidza, if possible.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, whose commander was General Milosevic, had in its area of responsibility these two locations, Lukavica and Ilidza? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge at that time and according to your memory, did those two places, Lukavica and Ilidza, communicate? How could I communicate with L?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did communicate with each other. How they did it, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, according to you, what's the distance between I and L?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 5 and 6 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So if you can just remember in your head where those two locations are.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I need the original map. We need to zoom back out, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: If you could keep in mind where Ilidza and Lukavica are, because they're going to be very small on the map once we have zoomed out.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So can we please display the map, and we don't need to tender this one. Please slightly zoom.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And could you please place an L on Lukavica again, if you can see it and locate it.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And an I on Ilidza. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: If you could please draw a line, a straight line, between those two.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did the units that were within the zone of responsibility of Ilidza and Lukavica move along the straight line? Could they do that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
